ElectionStudy.title: What each stock did in excess of the Ibovespa
ElectionStudy.intro: Every figure nets out the index move. What shows up in the table is company-specific — the political premium or discount the market assigned to it, not the tide that lifted or sank every boat.
ElectionStudy.footnote: The most useful reading is not the next-day column, but comparing the prior 90 sessions with the year after. When a stock rallies hard beforehand and gives it back later, the market bought the expectation and sold the fact.

pre90.label: 90 sessions before
pre90.description: The election race itself. This is where the market recalculates probabilities and moves prices.

d1.label: 1st session after 1st round
d1.description: The immediate reaction to the result. Measures how surprised the market was.

d5.label: 5 sessions after 1st round
d5.description: The first week, after the initial shock noise fades.

runoffD1.label: 1st session after runoff
runoffD1.description: The reaction to the definitive winner.

post60.label: 60 sessions after runoff
post60.description: The government transition: economic team, early fiscal signals.

post250.label: 1 year after runoff
post250.description: The real test. Election euphoria either becomes a structural rally — or evaporates.

2014.pricedIn: Alternation rally: the market rose hard from March to September as polls suggested a change of government.
2014.note: The limiting case of an election priced in too early. The reversal came on election night, and state-controlled names gave back the premium they had built up.

2018.pricedIn: A liberal agenda with Paulo Guedes at Finance, privatization promises, and pension reform.
2018.note: The result confirmed the scenario the market had been buying since September, so the rally came before — and continued after.

2022.pricedIn: A Lula win widely expected in the polls, with doubt about the new term's fiscal anchor.
2022.note: The election itself barely moved prices. The damage came later, with the Transition PEC — showing that what matters is what the government does, not who wins.

ScenarioSimulator.chooseIntro: Each scenario is a set of shocks over a 6-month horizon. Adjust the controls to build your own.
ScenarioSimulator.resultsIntro: Projection built from each stock's historical betas. A sensitivity reading, not a forecast: it shows how these companies tended to react to similar shocks.

ibov.label: Ibovespa
ibov.help: The move of the market as a whole.

selic.label: Selic
selic.help: Change in the policy rate, in percentage points.

usdbrl.label: Dollar
usdbrl.help: An increase means a weaker real.

brent.label: Brent crude
brent.help: Commodity price on the international market.

ust10y.label: 10-year Treasury
ust10y.help: US long rates: a rise tends to drain capital from emerging markets.

neutral.name: Nothing changes
neutral.summary: The election confirms what was already in the price. Rates, FX, and oil stay put. Serves as a baseline to compare everything else against.

promarket.name: Pro-market turn
promarket.summary: Outcome read as favorable to fiscal discipline and privatizations. The real strengthens, the yield curve rallies, and Copom can cut the Selic.

fiscalanchor.name: Continuity with a fiscal anchor
fiscalanchor.summary: The elected government presents a fiscal plan the market finds credible. The rally is smaller than in a full turn, but the rates channel works the same way.

fiscaldrift.name: No fiscal anchor
fiscaldrift.summary: Public spending accelerates, debt worsens, and the market demands a premium. The real weakens and the central bank starts hiking again.

oilshock.name: Oil shock
oilshock.summary: Brent spikes on geopolitical tension. Good for producers, bad for inflation — and reopens the debate over Petrobras pricing policy.

riskoff.name: Global risk-off
riskoff.summary: The problem comes from abroad: US long rates rise, the dollar strengthens, and foreign capital leaves emerging markets. The election becomes a sideshow.
